Title: Multi-process lost update / duplicate-ID vulnerability
Root Cause: No cross-process coordination; two `node server.js` processes against the same db.json each read/write independently with the last writer silently discarding the other's changes
Fix Summary: Added an OS-level exclusive single-instance lock (db.json.lock, O_EXCL) claimed at module load, before the first read of db.json. A second process against the same db.json is refused at startup with a clear error. Stale locks from a crashed process are auto-reclaimed (PID liveness check) - re-verified across restart/stale-lock/abnormal-termination scenarios at the Phase 1 Closure Gate. Windows does not support external graceful-shutdown signal delivery to this console process (confirmed: taskkill without /F, process.kill(pid,'SIGTERM'), and .NET CloseMainWindow() all fail to invoke the registered SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers) - the stale-lock auto-recovery is the compensating control for this platform limitation, and is proven reliable. This closes the audit's EXACT reproduction scenario; full cross-process ACID still requires the Stage 2 database migration (see ERP-001). MITIGATED, not architecturally resolved.

Title: Account lockout is completely non-functional - failed-login bookkeeping is silently rolled back
Root Cause: Phase ERP-059A) + FIXED (remaining 12-site audit-durability gap
Affected Module: Phase ERP-059B) - verified on isolated servers only; see Production-Data-Incident note in Test column
Affected Function: /api/login is legacy-dispatched (not on the modern registerMutationRoute framework), so it is wrapped by server.js's legacy-dispatch withTransaction() boundary. withTransaction() unconditionally restores DB to its pre-request snapshot whenever the wrapped handler's result has ok:false - a defensive rule that is correct for ordinary business-rule rejections (which validate before their first mutation) but wrong for /api/login, which INTENTIONALLY mutates user.failedLoginCount/lockedUntil as the entire point of returning ok:false on a wrong password. The mutation and its save() were proven (via live instrumented reproduction) to execute correctly in memory and on disk - then a LATER save() from the transaction wrapper's own rollback overwrites the file back to the pre-request state, erasing both the counter and the loginHistory DENY record.
Fix Summary: /api/login route (server.js), withTransaction() (domain.js)
column11: FIXED (Phase ERP-059A, 2026-09-10) via Option A: /api/login excluded from the legacy-dispatch withTransaction() wrapper entirely (mirrors the existing isModernRoute bypass). Verified: 5 wrong passwords now correctly lock the account (423), lock persists across restart, expires correctly, survives concurrent attempts, no password/hash leakage, no session on failure. A dedicated transaction-contract test proves 5 ordinary business rejections (finance/procurement/inventory/workflow) still roll back correctly - the fix is provably scoped to login only. Blast-radius RE-classified and CORRECTED: roughly half of the forensic gate's ~22 'presumed affected' sites were false positives (successful-rejection actions returning ok:true); the true remaining scope is 12 call sites (6 live-confirmed broken this phase: ReversalRejected/Finance, SupplierBillThreeWayMatchBypassRejected/Procurement, InventoryAdjustmentRejected/Inventory, UserCreationRejected/Security, MasterDataImportBatchRejected/Audit - plus the now-fixed login itself; 6 more structurally confirmed but not live-tested: GRNRejected, PurchaseReturnRejected, MaterialIssueRejected, SiteReturnRejected, JobWorkScrapRejected, RestoreRejectedValidationFailed/ChecksumMismatch). Option B (persist-on-failure semantics in withTransaction, to close the remaining 12) recommended but NOT implemented in Phase ERP-059A, per that phase's explicit 'do not over-remediate' scope. FIXED in Phase ERP-059B (2026-09-10): a narrow, explicit 'durableFailureAudit' field added to withTransaction()'s existing rollback branch - a handler may attach ONE audit payload to its ok:false result, written via the existing logAudit() AFTER the snapshot restore has already completed, so it cannot carry any business mutation along with it (by construction, not by convention).
